# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–3 (Complete and Final – Updated 57)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer of first year; autumn of first year; narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford; Also: Chiswick Mall (Miss Pinkerton's academy location), Hammersmith, Soho, Thames, England, Oxford, Chiswick Church, Buxton, Kensington turnpike, Russell Square, London, India (Boggley Wollah, Ramgunge, Calcutta)
- **Current Setting Details**: River crossing at Gulton and Quenwick; forge with chalked crooked sun on wall; wind from water with salt and tar smell; gulls quarreling over fish heads by steps; smoke from chimneys lying flat over fields; frost silvering hedges overnight; turnip cart passing well; light going early as spring approaches; children chasing hoop down lane; road all ruts and puddles after thaw; market town of Bryngate; hill farms of Coldcombe and Mirecombe; bees humming in lavender behind parsonage; bell for vespers ringing thinly across roofs; rain threatening since morning but holding off

## Main Characters

**Dorothea and Will Ladislaw (Married)**
- Engaged after Will's return to Middlemarch; Will had arms around her when she spoke of living on her seven-hundred-a-year fortune
- **Marriage**: Now married; has a little boy (infant); Celia expressed alarm that Will would hinder visits and concern about Dorothea's parenting and their fear she would die
- **Family Reconciliation**: Initial family opposition gradually resolved; Mr. Brooke corresponded with Will and Dorothea, sent invitation to Grange during months of correspondence while presupposing to Sir James Chettam that entail-cutting intention maintained; Mr. Brooke conveyed stronger sense than ever of reasons for energetic step against low blood mixture in Brooke heir
- **Visits to Family**: Established pattern of at least two visits yearly to Grange; Dorothea and Will's cousins at Freshitt enjoyed playing with their two cousins visiting Tipton
- **Sir James's Enduring Opposition**: Never ceased regarding second marriage as mistake; became tradition in Middlemarch that she married sickly clergyman old enough to be father, then within year gave up estate to marry his cousin—young, propertyless, not well-born
- **Will's Relationship with Sir James**: Never liked each other; on footing of reciprocal tolerance
- **Dorothea's Life Assessment**: Acts not ideally beautiful but mixed result of young, noble impulse struggling amidst imperfect social conditions; finely touched spirit had fine issues though not widely visible; full nature spent itself in channels with no great name on earth; effect of her being on those around her incalculably diffusive; growing good of world partly dependent on unhistoric acts and those who lived faithfully hidden life

**Mary Garth and Fred Garth (Married)**
- **Present Status**: Inhabit Stone Court; on sunny days seen in white-haired placidity at open window from which Mary once had been ordered to look out for Mr. Lydgate in old Peter Featherstone's days
- **Marriage Achievement**: Solid mutual happiness; Fred makes no failure; becomes rather distinguished in county as theoretic and practical farmer; produces work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding" winning high congratulations at agricultural meetings
- **Fred's Character Development**: Remains unswervingly steady some years after marriage; told Mary happiness half owing to Farebrother who gave strong pull-up at right moment; never wholly free from misled hopefulness—crop yields and profits usually fell below estimate; kept love of horsemanship but rarely allowed hunting days; gradually saved enough to become owner of stock and furniture at Stone Court
- **Fred's Feelings**: Had pleasant vision on winter evenings of bright hearth; sorry for other men who could not have Mary for wife, especially Mr. Farebrother; told Mary magnanimously "He was ten times worthier of you than I was"; Mary answered he could do better without her, but Fred would have been curate in debt
- **Children**: Three boys only; youngest very much what her father must have been when wore round jacket; Mary brings forth little formal teaching, alarming Mrs. Garth lest never well grounded; nevertheless children found quite forward when went to school

**Rebecca Sharp (Miss Becky)**
- **Age and Background**: Age seventeen when arrived at Miss Pinkerton's academy as articled pupil; now nineteen years old; **unused to the art of deceiving** and making her own experience; father was artist and drawing teacher at academy—clever man, pleasant companion, prone to debt and tavern; beat wife and daughter when drunk; died after third delirium tremens attack; mother was French opera-girl; Rebecca claims descent from noble Entrechats family of Gascony; as advanced in life, ancestors increased in rank
- **Appearance**: Small, slight person; pale, sandy-haired with large, odd, attractive eyes habitually cast down; dressed in white with bare shoulders described as picture of youth, unprotected innocence, and humble virgin simplicity
- **Languages and Accomplishments**: Speaks French with purity and Parisian accent; musician and good linguist when arrived at academy; practiced music incessantly; teaches music to younger pupils
- **Departure from Chiswick**: Said farewell to Miss Pinkerton in French ("Mademoiselle, je viens vous faire mes adieux"); threw Dixonary at Miss Jemima in act of defiance; departed carriage while other students wept; sank back in easy frame of mind; nobody cried for Miss Sharp leaving
- **Character**: Had dismal precocity of poverty; many a dun she had talked to; many a tradesman she had coaxed into good-humour; showed no will or strength rivaling Miss Pinkerton's authority; never had been a girl, was woman since age eight; expressed inexpressible envy at advantages of wealthier young women; determined to make connected plans for future; expressed hatred of Miss Pinkerton and Chiswick
- **Demands for Position**: Demanded "Give me a sum of money and get rid of me—or get me a good place as governess in a nobleman's family"; indentures ultimately cancelled after battle lasting several months
- **The Crisp Affair**: Reverend Mr. Crisp, fresh from Oxford and curate to Vicar Flowerdew, fell in love after glance across Chiswick Church; proposed something like marriage in intercepted note; Mrs. Crisp summoned from Buxton and carried off her son; **rumor claims** tart-woman hinted great deal more than public knowledge; his letter in answer to another letter (**truth unknown**)
- **Recommendation**: Miss Pinkerton recommended Miss Sharp for governess position with Sir Pitt Crawley's family, stating "I cannot find fault with Miss Sharp's conduct except to myself; must allow her talents and accomplishments are of high order"
- **Visit to Russell Square**: Invited by friend Miss Sedley to pass week at her home before entering governess duties; at Kensington turnpike, Amelia had not forgotten companions but dried tears, blushed at young officer of Life Guards; before carriage arrived in Russell Square, great conversation about Drawing-room, powder, hoops, presentation, Lord Mayor's ball
- **At Sedley Household**: Showed Rebecca over every room, books, piano, dresses, necklaces, braces, laces, gimcracks; insisted Rebecca accept white cornelian and turquoise rings and sprigged muslin too small for Amelia; determined to present white Cashmere shawl (Joseph just brought two from India); Rebecca said with perfect truth "it must be delightful to have a brother"; easily got pity of tender-hearted Amelia for being orphan without friends or kindred
- **Regarding Joseph Sedley**: Upon seeing two magnificent Cashmere shawls brought from India, Rebecca vowed and protested she expected to see Amelia's nephews and nieces; was quite disappointed Joseph not married; said she doted so on little children; in her heart determined "If Mr. Joseph Sedley is rich and unmarried, why should I not marry him? I have only a fortnight, to be sure, but there is no harm in trying"; redoubled caresses to Amelia; kissed white cornelian necklace as she put it on; vowed never to part with it
- **Meeting Joseph**: Went downstairs with arm round friend's waist; so agitated at drawing-room door could hardly find courage to enter; said to friend "Feel my heart, how it beats, dear!"; was dressed in white with bare shoulders as white as snow
- **At Dinner**: Thought "I must be very quiet and very much interested about India"; when served chili at dinner, thought it something cool; put one in mouth and found it hotter than curry; laid down fork crying "Water, for Heaven's sake, water!"; swallowed mortification and said with comical, good-humoured air about Arabian Nights and cream-tarts in Persia, asking if they put cayenne into cream-tarts in India

**Lydgate and Rosamond**: Made final resolution to leave Middlemarch; Dorothea sent letter with check for thousand pounds; Lydgate has accepted narrowed lot with sad resignation; full of timid care for wife; Rosamond meek enough to nestle under old despised shelter; has sent daughters away to board at school on coast

**Caleb Garth**: Had tender concern for Mary's contentment; expresses belief woman must not force her heart; voice shook perceptibly when speaking of Fred and Mary's marriage

## Secondary Characters

**Miss Amelia Sedley**: Pupil at Miss Pinkerton's academy; friends with Miss Sharp; exceedingly alarmed at Miss Sharp's insubordination; parted from friends at departure; now in seventeenth year about to leave school; invited Miss Sharp to pass week at her home; happy and handsome girl; tends white cornelian necklace, Cashmere shawls, sprigged muslin, braces for Joseph; embroidered beautiful pair of braces for brother; seemed to suffer thinking poor Rebecca suffering too much at dinner

**Joseph Sedley**: Amelia's brother, twelve years her senior; in East India Company's Civil Service; appeared in Bengal division of East India Register as collector of Boggley Wollah (honourable and lucrative post); lived alone at Boggley Wollah for about eight years scarcely seeing Christian face except twice yearly; caught liver complaint and returned to Europe; did not live with family in London but had lodgings of own like gay young bachelor; before India was too young for town pleasures, plunged into them on return with considerable assiduity; drove horses in Park, dined at fashionable taverns, frequented theatres, made appearance at opera in tights and cocked hat; **very stout, puffy man in buckskins and Hessian boots with several immense neckcloths rising to nose, red striped waistcoat, apple green coat with steel buttons almost as large as crown pieces** (morning costume of dandy of those days); reading paper by fire when girls entered; bounced off arm-chair, blushed excessively, hid face in neckcloths; continued huge clattering at poker and tongs, puffing and blowing, turning red as yellow face would allow; in serious alarm at embroidered braces; plunged at bell-rope which came away in hand; said "For heaven's sake see if my buggy's at the door. I CAN'T wait. I must go"; burst out laughing at Rebecca's chili incident (coarse man from Stock Exchange loving practical jokes); echoed paternal laugh

**Miss Jemima**: Daughter of Miss Pinkerton; pulled Miss Sharp away in great alarm after Dixonary incident; embraced Miss Sedley saying "Come away, Becky"; almost fainted with terror

**Miss Pinkerton**: Proprietor of academy at Chiswick Mall (the "Hammersmith Semiramis"); large Roman-nosed head with large solemn turban; tall as grenadier; does not understand French; said "Miss Sharp, I wish you a good morning"; waved hand by way of adieu; tossed up turban indignantly; said "Heaven bless you, my child" embracing Amelia while scowling over girl's shoulder at Miss Sharp; called Minerva in narrative; had no will or strength like little apprentice; attempted to scold Miss Sharp in public but Rebecca's French answers routed her

**Miss Swartz**: Parlour-boarder at Miss Pinkerton's academy; made hysterical YOOPS during farewell scene

**Reverend Mr. Crisp**: Fresh from Oxford; curate to Vicar Flowerdew of Chiswick; fell in love with Miss Sharp; proposed in intercepted note; carried off by mother from Buxton

**Stenworth, Lindson, Hollwood, Orlwood, Wexwood, Corrett Families**: Multiple family members in minor scenes; named: Nynelle Stenworth (married Halan Hollwood, gave birth to Rozek); Orbin, Orrine, Feena Stenworth; Halan, Rozek Hollwood; Colan, Islis, Ridette, Maric Lindson; Seena, Fedette Orlwood; Cotho Hollwood (won jade mirror from Fedette at cards fairly); Pebin Wexwood (hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step), Daena Wexwood, Ilrine, Ilzek Wexwood; Eldette Corrett, Cobin Corrett (swore to Pebin to repair chapel roof at Wilhaven), Thidrek Corrett, Rida Corrett; Thiena (watched clouds and predicted rain wrongly); Jolia (complained of aching back)

**Mr. Sedley**: Amelia and Joseph's father; coarse man from Stock Exchange

## Rumors and Unverified Claims Preserved
- Wife of Ridan Corrett confided to Ilzek Wexwood that bridge toll at Salwick skimmed every month
- Gossip claimed Thidrek Corrett and Rira Stenworth had been wed in secret
- Cotho Hollwood quit Wilhaven after quarrel, took lodgings in Coldcombe
- Tart-woman hinted there was great deal more than public knowledge regarding Mr. Crisp and Miss Sharp; his letter in answer to another letter (**truth unknown**)
- Lindson blood debt to Hollmere; Lindson mill ledger rewritten after flood; Salford granary fire set on purpose; old abbey at Salford second cellar; Bryngate pastures deed forged; silver chest buried beneath Mirecombe well; Quenwick chapel vault opens only for living person with jade ring and oak comb; Dunholt toll bridge belonged to Wexwood family
